newsitem.title: JAPAN: Current yen/dlr range no problem for Japan - Utsumi.
newsitem.headline: Current yen/dlr range no problem for Japan - Utsumi.

text.p: A range of 110-120 yen to the dollar is not a problem for Japan but a yen weaker than 125 yen to the greenback would be excessive, a former Japanese vice finance minister said on Tuesday.

Makoto Utsumi, who was vice minister for international affairs at Japan's Ministry of Finance (MOF) and is now a professor at Keio University in Tokyo, also told Reuters Financial Television in an interview that Japanese government bonds (JGBs) are trading at "bubble" levels and prices are likely to undergo a downward correction due to increased economic activity in Japan.

On foreign exchange levels, Utsumi said a range of 110 to 120 yen to the dollar was not a problem for Japan but added that "to go back to 125 (yen) is excessive". The dollar has been trading above 117 yen this week.
"Basically, the bond prices are more or less (a) bubble," Utsumi said. "It doesn't reflect the reality... Sooner or later the correction should happen reflecting Japanese economic activities."
Utsumi said strength in U.S. and European equity markets had come amid weakness in European economic fundamentals and turmoil in Asian markets.

With these conditions, Utsumi said he did not understand why Japanese investors were so "excessively cautious" about putting money into Japanese equities, but added that "sooner or later" there would also be a correction in stock prices.
Utsumi would not comment on how significant a correction could be expected from current levels of the Nikkei average, which are near calendar 1997 highs.
Such a change would see funds flowing into the Japanese equity markets. "The shift towards the Japanese stock market is a possibility," Utsumi said.
Utsumi would not comment on the extent of the correction to stock price levels.

Turning to the subject of Thailand's financial woes, Utsumi said he expected the Japanese government and private institutions to extend loans if the International Monetary Fund (IMF) was part of cooperative funding efforts.
"Japanese Ministry of Finance officials are recognising what they should do on these problems and in cooperation with the IMF, especially the IMF, they are ready to help," he said.

"But without any policy commitment, Japan alone cannot do anything," Utsumi said. "I think it (lending) might happen because they have already a lot of exposure and it's in their own interest to do that."
Earlier on Tuesday, Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka welcomed Thailand's moves to start discussions with the IMF on how to overcome problems in the Thai economy.
